title: Signal International (Indian H-2B workers)
summary: After Hurricane Katrina, Signal International used the H-2B program to bring nearly 500 men from India to work as welders and pipefitters in Mississippi and Texas; recruiters promised green cards and permanent residency, and workers paid $10,000–$20,000 or more in fees. Workers were charged $1,050 a month to live in overcrowded, guarded company camps. In February 2015 a New Orleans federal jury awarded $14 million to five workers, finding Signal and businesses of lawyer Malvern C. Burnett and recruiter Sachin Dewan liable for labor trafficking, fraud, racketeering and discrimination. In 2015 Signal agreed to a $20 million settlement resolving the SPLC-coordinated suits, including a $5 million EEOC settlement.

journey.note: Recruiters promised good jobs, green cards and permanent residency in exchange for large fees.
Workers were housed in overcrowded company camps at $1,050 a month and paid below-market wages.
Signal also employed the workers at its Orange, Texas facility.
A federal jury awarded $14 million to five workers after a four-week trial.

lures.quote_or_description: Workers paid "$10,000 and $20,000 or more in recruitment fees and other costs".
Recruiters promised green cards and permanent US residency, but workers came on temporary H-2B visas.
Many sold property or took on family debt to pay fees and could not change jobs without losing their investment.
Workers were forced to pay $1,050 a month to live in overcrowded, unsanitary, guarded camps, up to 24 men per unit.
